newsitem.title: UK: Burmah rises, analysts see scope for more.
newsitem.headline: Burmah rises, analysts see scope for more.

text.p: Fuelled by a 13 percent profit rise, Burmah Castrol shares rose sharply on Monday with many analysts saying there is plenty of scope for more advances.
"In principle it is still a buy," said Elisabeth Butler at Panmure Gordon. "I have a value on it well in excess of 11 pounds, so it's still cheap."
Burmah shares climbed 19 pence to 1069 pence.

Many analysts consider Burmah a growth stock, which is cashing in on its strong presence in fast growing Asian markets. The company itself said earlier that its Castrol lubricants in Asia are growing in volume terms at twice the market rate.
"It is a cheap stock, growing more than the market, but with a sub-market multiple," said Paul Spedding at Kleinwort Benson.
Burmah Castrol reported a rise in first-half net income before exceptional gains to 67.7 million from 59.9 million, in line with market forecasts.
Operating income in the lubricants sector rose by seven percent to 100.8 million stg with Burmah saying growth of the Castrol brand in Asia looked set to continue.
"Castrol just keeps churning out money," said Butler.
The strength of the Castrol brand name gave the shares an early boost in the beginning of the year.
But investors' interest unexpectedly petered out after April when the company reported its full-year results.

Shares languished through the summer months, but suddenly regained momentum in August following several positive analysts' comments. Burmah climbed from 978 pence on July 23 to peak at a closing high of 1069 on August 16.

Bruce Evers at Henderson Crosthwaite was one of few analysts sceptical about the renewed enthusiasm for Burmah, pointing to difficult conditions in more mature markets such as Europe and Germany in particular.
"There is always one bit of the business that doesn't do that well," he said, adding he considered Burmah fairly priced at the moment.
Burmah said earlier that the German economy seemed to have the worst behind it, adding this could help its lubricants and chemicals operations next year.
Operating profit at the chemical division rose seven percent to 32.2 million in the first half of 1996.

Burmah has set up a meeting with analysts in November to detail its strategy in the chemicals sector, which has been heavily criticised after the company made a big acquisition in 1991, just when the market was heading for a downturn.
Sarah Muscat at Yamaichi said she considered Burmah shares worth buying ahead of the November meeting, which she expected would help restore full confidence in the company's strategy.
"We are looking for the company to give us a clear picture then," she said.
